flashcards.q: What is the skip-gram negative sampling objective, and why replace the full softmax?
flashcards.a: log σ(v'_wO · v_wI) + Σ_{i=1}^k E[log σ(−v'_wi · v_wI)]. Full softmax needs O(V) dot products per example (infeasible at vocab scale); negative sampling turns it into O(k) binary classification between real and k sampled fake pairs.

flashcards.q: What noise distribution does Word2Vec's negative sampling use, and why?
flashcards.a: P_n(w) ∝ count(w)^0.75 (the 3/4 power). Dampens the dominance of extremely frequent words among negative samples while still oversampling frequent words relative to uniform -- an empirical finding, not derived from first principles.

flashcards.q: CBOW vs skip-gram: mechanism and when each wins?
flashcards.a: CBOW predicts center word from averaged context (faster, one prediction/window, better on frequent words). Skip-gram predicts each context word from center individually (slower, better on rare words and small datasets since it doesn't dilute rare words into an average).

flashcards.q: What did Levy & Goldberg (2014) prove about SGNS, and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: Skip-gram with negative sampling implicitly factorizes a word-context PMI matrix shifted by -log(k): v_wI · v'_wO ≈ PMI(wI,wO) − log(k). It's the theoretical bridge showing Word2Vec (implicit, prediction-based) and GloVe (explicit, count-based) solve structurally related problems.

flashcards.q: What is GloVe's objective function and weighting function f(x)?
flashcards.a: J = Σ f(X_ij)(w_i·w̃_j + b_i + b̃_j − log X_ij)². f(x) = (x/x_max)^α if x<x_max else 1, with x_max=100, α=0.75 -- prevents very frequent co-occurrences dominating the loss while giving zero weight to co-occurrences that never happened.

flashcards.q: How does fastText compute a word vector, and why does that fix OOV words?
flashcards.a: A word's vector is the SUM of its character n-gram vectors (n=3-6) plus a whole-word token. An unseen word decomposes into n-grams likely seen in training, so summing their vectors gives a usable representation -- Word2Vec/GloVe have no vector at all for unseen words.

flashcards.q: Why can a static embedding not represent polysemy, structurally?
flashcards.a: Training assigns exactly one vector per word type, aggregating evidence from every context seen during training into a single point -- there's no mechanism to condition the output on the current sentence, since the vector is computed once offline and looked up, not computed at inference time.

flashcards.q: What broke static embeddings' dominance, and which models did it?
flashcards.a: ELMo (2018, BiLSTM hidden states per token) then BERT (2018, transformer + masked LM) computed a different vector per token occurrence conditioned on the sentence, fixing polysemy structurally and beating static embeddings on nearly every downstream benchmark.

flashcards.q: Name four concrete reasons static embeddings still make sense in production.
flashcards.a: Latency (microsecond lookup vs ms forward pass), cost (precompute once vs pay per request), interpretability (fixed, auditable nearest neighbors), and edge/on-device or high-QPS real-time systems where a transformer forward pass doesn't fit the budget.

flashcards.q: What is item2vec/prod2vec and what's its limitation for true cold start?
flashcards.a: Applying skip-gram with negative sampling to sequences of user-item interactions (browsing/booking) instead of text sentences -- co-occurring items get similar vectors. It doesn't solve true cold start: an item with zero interactions gets no vector, same as Word2Vec's OOV problem for text.

flashcards.q: Why is mixing embedding vectors from two separate training runs in the same similarity index a bug?
flashcards.a: Embedding spaces from separate training runs have arbitrary orientation -- only relative geometry within a single run is meaningful. Mixing runs produces nonsensical nearest neighbors even though each individual run is internally valid.
